https://www.dw.com/en/uk-reports-major-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NM3E The US Air Force has used the British base for attacks against Iran Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS Advertisement British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning. The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines. UK police blocked roads leading to the Fairford airbase Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS Police said the bomb disposal units were "currently examining a number of vehicles" in Whelford. Residents of multiple properties in the village have been taken to a nearby leisure center. "A cordon is currently in place but we'd like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained," British police said. Police also said several men were "arrested on suspicion of offences the ​Explosives Act" but would not confirm the arrests were connected to the incident near the base. Officials stay tight-lipped A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families." This Fairford base gates was blocked by construction machinery Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS The background for the incident was not immediately clear. The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran , with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland , and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport , which its authorities attributed to Russia. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crpd.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Many opposition lawmakers, including the Congress party's Rahul Gandhi, were stopped midway as they marched towards the Election Commission headquarters By Abhishek Dey Published 6 October 2026 Police in Delhi detained several opposition lawmakers as they tried to march demanding the chief election commissioner resign over a controversial voter roll revision. Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and other MPs were forced into a police bus. Released shortly after, they resumed their march and began a sit-in near Election Commission headquarters. It is the latest escalation in a growing row over a nationwide revision of voter rolls. Opposition parties accuse Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of overseeing a process that could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), an allegation both the BJP and Election Commission have rejected. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Security officials blocked the roads from India's parliament to the election commission headquarters "Some of the MPs tried to take some other roads to the Election Commission building. We have officers stationed at multiple points, from where the protesters were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC. The police did not disclose how many lawmakers had been detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from a range of parties participated in the march. Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October. At the centre of the controversy is the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country. The Election Commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide. Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and accuse the poll body of conducting the process improperly. The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the Election Commission's name without their knowledge. According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data. Some concerns were linked directly to the electoral roll revision programme. The Election Commission, a three-member body comprising the chief election commissioner and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously. The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of a controversy over allegations of manipulating voter rolls Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge described three demands as "non-negotiable": Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting. Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India's lower house of parliament, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign." The BJP condemned the protests. BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission. The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners. The petition argues that Kumar exercised powers that belong to the commission collectively and seeks a ruling that any such actions were unauthorised. The court indicated that Election Commission decisions must be taken either unanimously or by majority vote and suggested that decisions could be set aside if found to have bypassed that process. However, it declined to suspend Kumar at this stage, saying it would first hear the Election Commission's response and examine relevant records. The BBC has contacted the Election Commission for comment on Tuesday's protest.
